notes.h: Properties of light and their application (Higher Level only)
points: Reflection: light rays bounce back from shiny surfaces such as mirrors, glazed tiles and white ceilings, which brightens a room.
Refraction: light rays bend as they pass through thick or ridged glass, such as glass bricks, which spreads light through a room.
Diffusion: light rays scatter when they pass through translucent material such as frosted glass, net curtains or fabric shades, giving soft light.
Absorption: dark, matt surfaces take in light rather than reflecting it, so a room with dark walls appears smaller and cosier.
Dispersion: a prism or crystal splits white light into its component colours, as in a crystal chandelier.

notes.h: Planning a lighting system (Higher Level only)
points: Plan the lighting at the design stage, so that outlets and fittings are positioned before construction begins.
Match the lighting to the function of the room: a kitchen needs bright task lighting at work surfaces, while a living room needs a softer mix of light.
Combine general, task and accent lighting, and use one or more focal points to set the atmosphere.
Balance natural and artificial light: the aspect of the room and the size of its windows determine how much daylight it receives.
Avoid glare by placing fittings away from the normal line of sight and by using shades that spread the light.
Allow flexibility with dimmers, timers and movable lamps so that the light can suit different activities and times of day.
Safety: use the correct voltage and fuse rating, install fittings correctly, and leave adequate space between the bulb and the shade.
Maintenance: fittings should be easy to clean, and bulbs and any replaceable parts should be easy to reach.
The colour of walls and ceilings affects the light in a room: pale colours reflect light, while dark colours absorb it.

notes.h: How energy-efficient lamps work (Higher Level only)
points: A filament bulb produces light by heating a tungsten filament, and most of the energy it uses is given off as heat.
Compact fluorescent lamp (CFL): electric current passes through argon gas and mercury vapour inside a looped glass tube, producing ultraviolet light.
A phosphor coating on the inside of the CFL tube converts the ultraviolet light into visible light.
CFLs use much less energy and last much longer than filament bulbs, but they cost more to buy and contain mercury, so they must be disposed of safely.
Light-emitting diode (LED): light is produced when electrons combine with gaps called holes in a semiconductor, and the colour depends on the semiconductor material.
LEDs use far less electricity than filament bulbs, start instantly, give off little heat and have a very long life.
Energy-saving use: dimmers, timers, motion sensors and switching off unneeded lights reduce the energy used by any lamp.
LED strips, bulbs and compact fittings are available in different colour temperatures and can be fitted into small or awkward spaces.
Sensor or motion-activated lighting switches on only when movement is detected, saving energy in halls, stairs and outdoor areas.
Smart lighting can be controlled from a phone or voice assistant to set schedules, dim the lights or change their colour.
Colour-changing LEDs and LED rope lighting create ambience and can be used as accent lighting.
Photovoltaic outdoor lights use a solar panel to charge a battery during the day and light up at night.
Dimmable LEDs need a compatible dimmer, and cheap LED lamps may flicker or give poor colour rendering.

notes.h: Types of lighting fitting by function (Higher Level only)
points: General lighting: central ceiling fittings such as semi-flush and flush fittings, pendants, chandeliers and rise-and-fall fittings.
Task lighting: under-cabinet lights, desk lamps and recessed downlights that light a specific activity.
Accent lighting: picture lights, wall brackets, track lights and spotlights that highlight a feature.

notes.h: Practical context: investigating contemporary lighting (Higher Level only)
points: Collect examples of contemporary lighting from magazines, brochures and shop visits, and record the type of fitting and its lamp, such as LED or CFL.
For each example, note whether it provides general, task or accent lighting, and what its packaging states about brightness and colour temperature.
Evaluate each example for energy efficiency, safety, maintenance and suitability for a named room.

keyTerms.definition: The bouncing back of light rays from a shiny or smooth surface.
The bending of light rays as they pass through a thick or ridged transparent material.
The scattering of light rays when they pass through a translucent material or strike a rough surface.
The taking in of light by a dark or matt surface, which then does not reflect it.
The splitting of white light into its component colours by a prism or crystal.
A low-energy lamp in which an electric current through mercury vapour produces ultraviolet light that a phosphor coating converts to visible light.
A semiconductor device that produces light directly from electricity with very little heat and a long life.
Overall lighting that provides a basic level of light throughout a room.
Focused lighting placed where a specific activity, such as cooking or reading, takes place.
Lighting used to highlight a particular feature or object in a room.
Uncomfortable brightness from a light source or reflective surface that interferes with seeing comfortably.

questions.prompt: Name three properties of light and give an example, from the home, of each.
questions.model: Any three of: reflection, with light bouncing off a mirror or glazed tile (2 marks); refraction, with light bending through a glass brick or thick glass (2 marks); diffusion, with light scattered through frosted glass or a translucent shade (2 marks). Also accepted: absorption by dark matt walls, and dispersion through a crystal chandelier.

questions.prompt: Discuss the principles to consider when planning a lighting system for a kitchen and dining area in a family home. Recommend two energy-efficient light sources for the room, explaining the underlying principle of each.
questions.model: Principles: use the room's natural light and aspect; match the lighting to each function, with task lighting over work surfaces and a softer general or accent light for dining; combine general, task and accent lighting around a focal point; avoid glare by careful positioning and shades; allow flexibility with dimmers and timers; ensure safety through correct voltage, fuse rating and fittings; choose fittings that are easy to clean and maintain; consider energy efficiency and the look of the fittings. Source 1, LED: a semiconductor produces light when electrons combine with holes, giving light directly from electricity with little heat and a long life, suitable for recessed, under-cabinet or pendant fittings. Source 2, CFL: current through argon and mercury vapour produces ultraviolet light, and a phosphor coating converts it to visible light; it uses much less energy than a filament bulb but contains mercury and needs safe disposal.
